b: In 1953, Nature published a two-page paper proposing that DNA is a double helix. It changed biology, and yet it was never externally peer-reviewed. The peer review system we have today did not become standard at Nature until 1973.

I read with interest the proposal published on Sensible Medicine by Howard Bauchner and Frederick Rivara to phase out human peer review in favor of AI-first reviews. I share their hope that technology can improve this process.

In fact, their argument was so good, I wonder if it can be extended. If, as they suggest, journals are to resemble a few editors plugging submitted manuscripts and data into a fancy version of Claude and asking if they are any good… can’t I just do that at home?
Technology has already driven academic journals online. The technology now exists that may, and I will argue ought to, finish the job and drive the modern academic journal extinct.

Academic journals have served three main functions during their history:

Dissemination: Journals get information to interested readers. Virologists subscribed to the Journal of Virology while neurologists subscribed to JAMA Neurology. Dissemination stopped being an issue a while ago thanks to the internet and PubMed, Google Scholar, email alerts, X, Bluesky, etc.

Filtering: It’s well known that JAMA Neurology is a good place to find important neurology studies, while a journal like Frontiers in Neurology tends to house “lower-impact” work. That’s why people check the JAMA Neurology homepage and not the Frontiers homepage.Journals are also supposed to filter out fraud, and while they assuredly catch some especially incompetent fraudsters, they have struggled in this area. Meanwhile, other fields publish new results on preprint servers with no peer review. Important results still spread quickly. Many of these manuscripts still appear in journals, months or years after making a big splash. This brings me to the last key role.

Credentialing: University departments and funding agencies appraise an academic’s work by examining his or her “publication record.” Since nobody wants to slow down and read the last five papers someone has published in depth, they just Google the impact factors of those journals and see if the number is big.

Because journals still do some of these things, people keep sending their work to them; and because they continue to receive most of the important science in medicine and biology, universities must keep paying their steep subscription fees.
Not only do I think AI can be an above-replacement peer reviewer, but I think it can do the rest of these things too. I’d like to outline just one way that this might work.
Imagining a future with no journals

Suppose authors posted their work as preprints the moment it was ready, and openly available AI reviewers evaluated it. A website could host several reputable AI evaluators, each publishing its scores daily for newly posted preprints. Readers could search for new findings, using a model that learned their field and interests, then compare evaluators, see where they agree and disagree, and read the full critiques behind every score. While we’re at it, why not have a comments section, where doctors and scientists can weigh in or link to related ideas?

Dissemination would be faster. Results would become public as soon as their authors are satisfied with them, not after they are collected, prepared for submission, and bounced through the peer-review process.

Filtering would be faster and more thorough. Every paper would get a critique that checks the full data, flags errors, and warns readers where data were not made available. Other scores could track originality and potential importance, not unlike what Bauchner and Rivara suggested.

Credentialing would become more aligned with the interests of science. A journal’s name on a CV is shorthand for peer reviewers’ approval. If those reviews are done by a fine-tuned AI model, your local academic department chair will have access to the same tools. Within a few hours, they could locate a candidate’s entire body of work instead of battling through paywalls and ascertain key factors that are routinely overlooked in today’s environment, such as whether they have made data available, whether that data is free of the fingerprints of fraud, and whether most of their experiments have an appropriate control group.
And… it would be cheap. Yes, AI is expensive, but have I mentioned that universities spend millions annually on bundles of journals from each of the major publishing houses?

Of course, there are important objections. Scores could be gamed, and having a few AI models in charge of a field could create blind spots. AI models will certainly carry biases of their own, though being less biased than humans, who have personal relationships with and interests in the people and ideas they review, is a low bar. There’s also the issue of “prompt injection,” in which bad actors, anticipating that their primary judge will be an AI, smuggle instructions into their manuscript or metadata that only an AI would notice. This has already been attempted and would certainly become common if this system goes mainstream. If all else fails, we’ll always have the human eye to fall back on, which we already do.
The system we have is imperfect, less permanent than it looks, and ripe for disruption. At journals like Nature, routine peer review is younger than the discovery of the double helix.

A scientific infrastructure that facilitates timely, useful, and truth-oriented information would not be a mere convenience. Many key discoveries in history came when seemingly unrelated ideas met in a single mind. Many others were delayed by years or decades because that meeting never happened. The scientific community should strive for a system that rewards good behavior and gets data to the right people quickly and efficiently.

Aidan McGinnis is an MD/PhD student on the West Coast. He is interested in neuroscience, critical appraisal, and science policy. He hopes to become a physician-scientist and run an academic lab focused on neurologic disease.
